cases.event: One winter, pages printed at the fictional shop {E} came out pale and patchy.
cases.q: What most likely caused the pages printed at {E} to come out pale?
restate: Pages printed at {E} came out pale and patchy, and the question asks why.
Something made the pages printed at {E} come out pale.
cases.answer: Ink that had thickened in the cold most likely caused the pale pages at {E}, because stiff ink does not spread evenly over the letters.
cases.sum: the evidence points to the cold, thickened ink as the reason the pages came out pale.
cases.myth: The pages at {E} came out pale because the paper forgot what it was supposed to print.
cases.mythClause: only pages printed on Mondays came out pale
cases.altText: Some printers suggested that the metal letters at {E} had worn out.
cases.patternQ: What pattern connects the temperature of the shop and the pages printed at {E}?
cases.patternA: Pages came out pale while the shop was cold and dark again once the ink warmed up, so the print quality followed the temperature.
cases.patternSum: the pages were pale while the shop was cold and dark once it warmed up.

prediction.text: At the start of winter, an apprentice predicted that only the oldest letters at {E} would print pale pages.
prediction.claim: only the oldest letters at {E} would print pale pages
prediction.whyNot: a brand-new set of letters printed pages that were just as pale

cases.observerNote: The printers kept a sample of every page they printed.

obs.text: The pale pages began in the week the shop's stove broke and the room fell to about {n0} degrees Celsius.
exps: the pale pages began when the shop turned cold, which points to the cold as the cause
the timing ties the problem to the broken stove, not to the letters
a sudden change in quality that matches a sudden change in temperature suggests a link

obs.text: The printer found that the ink in its pot had become stiff and lumpy.
exps: stiff, lumpy ink cannot spread evenly, so the letters pick up only patches of it
this shows how the cold caused pale pages, since thick ink does not coat the letters well
lumpy ink explains the patchy printing directly

obs.text: After the stove was fixed and the ink warmed up, the pages came out dark and clear again within {n1} days.
obs.tag: the pages after the shop warmed up
exps: the pages improved once the ink warmed, which is what would happen if cold ink were the cause
warming the shop fixed the problem, so the two are linked
once the cause was removed, the effect faded

obs.text: A brand-new set of metal letters printed pages that were just as pale.
exps: new letters cannot be worn out, yet they printed pale pages too
this rules out worn letters, because new ones had the same problem
if worn letters were the cause, the new set would have printed clearly
predExps: this directly contradicts the prediction, since new letters printed pale pages too
if only the oldest letters were the problem, the new set would print dark pages, but it did not
the prediction blamed old letters, but the problem stayed with new ones

obs.text: Under a magnifying glass, the edges of the old letters were still sharp and unworn.
exps: sharp edges show the letters were not worn out
this rules out worn letters, because their edges were still crisp
with the letters in good shape, the worn-letter explanation has nothing to stand on
